title: Introduce Kubernetes health-check failure
description: Project: Introduce Kubernetes health-check failure. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: Kubernetes uses three types of probes to manage pod lifecycle: liveness, readiness, and startup. A misconfigured probe can kill a healthy pod, route traffic to an unready instance, or block deployments indefinitely. This lesson covers how each probe type works, common configuration mistakes, and how to diagnose probe failures from events and metrics.

items: Liveness probe: detects if the application is running; failure causes a restart
Readiness probe: detects if the application can serve traffic; failure removes the pod from the service
Startup probe: delays liveness and readiness checks until the application has finished initialization
Probe thresholds: failureThreshold and successThreshold control how many attempts before a decision is made
Probe timing: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, and timeoutSeconds determine how aggressively Kubernetes probes

terms.definition: A Kubernetes probe that determines whether a container is running; failure triggers a restart of the container.
A Kubernetes probe that determines whether a container is ready to accept traffic; failure removes the pod from endpoints.
A Kubernetes probe that delays liveness and readiness checks until the application has completed startup.
A policy that limits how many pods of a replicated application can be unavailable simultaneously.
A deployment strategy that gradually replaces old pods with new ones while maintaining availability.

data.text: The most common mistake is setting liveness and readiness probes to the same endpoint with the same timing. A liveness probe that checks the database will restart the pod during a database blip, even if the pod could recover on its own. Readiness probes should be more sensitive than liveness probes because they affect traffic routing rather than process lifecycle.

data.title: Correct probe configuration
data.content: A deployment with distinct liveness, readiness, and startup probes:
data.code:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/live
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/ready
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 2
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2

startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/startup
    port: 8080
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 2

items: Check pod events with kubectl describe pod for ProbeError or Unhealthy events
Verify the probe path responds correctly from inside the cluster network
Confirm the probe timeout is shorter than the endpoint processing time
Check whether the probe port matches the container port and containerPort
Review pod logs around the time of restart to identify application-level errors

cards.title: Rolling update
cards.description: Gradually replaces old pods with new ones.
pros: No downtime if probes are correct
cons: Can cause resource spikes during rollout

cards.title: Recreate
cards.description: Tears down all old pods before starting new ones.

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.description: Switches traffic between two complete environments.

data.caption: Kubernetes pod lifecycle managed by liveness, readiness, and startup probes
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Pod scheduled] --> B{Startup probe passes?}
    B -->|No| C[Restart container]
    B -->|Yes| D[Liveness + Readiness active]
    D --> E{Readiness passes?}
    E -->|No| F[Remove from service endpoints]
    E -->|Yes| G[Add to service endpoints]
    D --> H{Liveness fails?}
    H -->|Yes| I[Kill and recreate pod]
    H -->|No| J[Continue serving]
    F --> K[Wait for readiness recovery]
    K --> E
    I --> A

    note right of B
        Startup probe gives slow-starting
        apps time before liveness kills them.
    end note

    note right of H
        Liveness is for broken processes,
        not for overloaded dependencies.
    end note

data.title: Liveness probes should not check downstream dependencies
data.text: A liveness probe that checks a database or external API will restart the pod whenever that dependency has a blip, even if the pod itself is healthy. Liveness should verify the process is running; readiness should verify dependencies are reachable.

items.question: Why is my pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff?
items.answer: Check the startup probe failureThreshold. If the application takes longer to start than the total startup window, Kubernetes kills and restarts it. Increase failureThreshold or fix the slow startup.

items.question: Why does traffic stop reaching my pod?
items.answer: The readiness probe is likely failing. Describe the pod and look for Unhealthy events. Verify the readiness endpoint is accessible from the cluster network and responds within the timeout.

items.question: Should I use TCP sockets instead of HTTP probes?
items.answer: TCP probes are useful for non-HTTP services such as databases, but they only verify the port is open, not that the application can serve requests. Prefer HTTP probes for web services; use TCP probes only as a fallback.

data.title: Diagnose and fix a probe misconfiguration
data.description: A pod is repeatedly restarting and failing its health checks. The readiness probe endpoint checks a database that is temporarily unavailable. Diagnose the issue and propose a fix.
steps: Use kubectl describe pod to identify which probe is failing
Determine whether liveness or readiness is the culprit
Propose separate endpoints for liveness and readiness
Adjust timing and thresholds to tolerate brief dependency unavailability
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a corrected probe configuration that prevents unnecessary restarts while still routing traffic away from unhealthy pods.

data.title: Summary
points: Use distinct endpoints for liveness, readiness, and startup probes
Liveness should not depend on downstream services
Startup probes protect slow-starting applications from premature kills
Diagnose probe failures from kubectl describe and pod events
Test probe configurations in staging under dependency failures
data.takeaway: Kubernetes probes are the safety net that keeps deployments healthy. A senior engineer configures them deliberately because a bad probe can turn a recoverable error into a cascading restart storm.
